title: Self-Attention
text:
Introduction
In the project Recognize Handwritten Digits by CNN, we used a CNN network to do the classification. And in the project COVID-19 Cases Prediction, which is a regression task, we directly used a full connected layer to make the predictions. They’re similar in some ways. We could think of their input as a vector, and our output is either a scalar in the regression tasks or a category in the classification tasks.
But what should we do when we’re dealing with a bunch of different vectors, and the number of vectors can change? And even the size of the vectors is different.


Code
flowchart LR
  A(a vector) --> B{Model}
  B --> C(Scalar or Class)

  D(a set of vectors) --> E{Model}
  E --> F(Scalars or Classes)





flowchart LR
  A(a vector) --> B{Model}
  B --> C(Scalar or Class)

  D(a set of vectors) --> E{Model}
  E --> F(Scalars or Classes)

title: Self-Attention
text:
Vector Set as Input

Text
Supposed that our input is a sentence. They’re different lengths, and they have different numbers of vocabularies. We can describe each vocabulary as a vector, so our input will be a set of vectors.
There are two methods we can represent our vocabularies as vectors.

One-Hot Encoding
Word Embedding: Give each word a vector containing semantic information. The embeddings of similar lexical words are similar.



Speech
We intercept a range from the speech, called Window. We can describe the window as a vector which called Frame. In general, the length of window is 25ms.
In the project Phoneme Classification, we did a such task.


Graph
We can think of a node in a graph as a vector. For example, in a social network, we can take each person’s profile—like age, profession, and so on—as a vector.

title: Self-Attention
text:
What’s the output?

Each vector has a corresponding label.
An intact sequence only has one label.
The model should decide the number of labels in the output by itself.

title: Self-Attention
text:
Sequence Labeling
Can we just use the fully connected network with each word as the input? It’s clearly not ideal because we’re not taking the context semantic information into account. In the project Phoneme Classification, we concatenate the current frame with its context, and feed it into a full-connected network.
But, when we face a problem that requires us to consider a whole sequence, how can we solve it? We cannot handle it with the method in phoneme classification, since the length of the sequence is different.
That’s why we introduce Self-Attention in here.

title: Self-Attention
text:
Self-Attention (star)


Code
flowchart LR
  A(Sequence) --> B(Self-attention)
  B --> C(word1 with context)
  B --> D(word2 with context)
  B --> E(word3 with context)
  B --> F(word4 with context)
  C --> G(FC) --> K( )
  D --> H(FC) --> L( )
  E --> I(FC) --> M( )
  F --> J(FC) --> N( )





flowchart LR
  A(Sequence) --> B(Self-attention)
  B --> C(word1 with context)
  B --> D(word2 with context)
  B --> E(word3 with context)
  B --> F(word4 with context)
  C --> G(FC) --> K( )
  D --> H(FC) --> L( )
  E --> I(FC) --> M( )
  F --> J(FC) --> N( )









fig1


As the figures shown in fig1, in the self-attention, \(b^1\) is generated by considering all the inputs \(a\). It’s the same as the phoneme classification. But, how does self-attention produce \(b^1\)?
There is a special mechanism in here. We find out which parts of the sequence are important and relevant for \(a^1\), which parts can determine the categorization of \(a^1\), etc. We define \(\alpha\) as the degree of relevance of \(a^1\).
How to calculate \(\alpha\)? (shown in fig2)



fig2



Dot Product

Two input vectors are multiplied by two different matrices, the left vector is multiplied by the matrix \(W^Q\) to get the matrix \(Q\), the right vector is multiplied by the matrix \(W^K\) to get the matrix \(K\). Then \(Q\) and \(K\) are dot-produced, that is, element-wise multiplied, and then added together to get a scalar \(\alpha\).

Additive

Two vectors through the \(W^Q\) and \(W^K\) get \(Q\) and \(K\), and then thrown to through an Activation Function and a Transform, and then get a scalar \(\alpha\).
We are likely to use the first method. Fig3 shows the details of calculating \(b^1\).



fig3


Let’s calculate the whole process.

Query, Key and Value
Query indicates what each element needs to focus on.
Key represents what each element can provide.
Value represents the information that each element provides to other elements.
Interpretation
We will use a library example to describe query, key and value. If we are in a library and we want to find a book. Query is the content you want to find; Key is the index or feature of the book that can describe the subject and content of a book, like a tag of a book; Value is the details of the book that can answer your demand, for example, book A is the algorithm of deep learning.
And their calculation is as follows:
\[
\begin{align*}
    Q &= A W^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_q}, \\
    K &= A W^K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}, \\
    V &= A W^V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v}
\end{align*}
\]
where \(A\) denotes the input matrix, and \(W\) denotes the weight matrix obtained by training.



Query, Key and Value




Attention Scores - \(\alpha\)
Interpretation
If we have an input \([Query, Key]\), we can find which book can match our demand. For example, given an input [‘machine learning’, ‘book1: the basic of machine learning’] which can match our demand. The administrator will assign a weight to each book to show its relevance to the demand. For example, Book1’s weight is 0.1 (low relevance) and Book2’s weight is 0.7 (high relevance).
\[
\begin{align*}
    \text{Attention}(Q, K)=\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}
\end{align*}
\]
In general, we will access a softmax behind Attention Scores. So, its calculation shows as follows:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \text{Attention\_weights}(Q, K) &= \text{Softmax} \left( \frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)
\end{align*}
\]
The process shows in Attention Scores.



Attention Scores




Output Matrix - \(B\)
Interpretation
We take the content of book (Value) based on the weight. For example, the administrator will pay more attention on the books that matches your demand, and ignore the books you don’t need.
\[
\begin{align*}
    \text{Output}=\text{Attention\_weights}\cdot V
\end{align*}
\]
The process shows in Output Matrix.



Output Matrix




The Whole Process



Whole Process

title: Self-Attention
text:
Multi-head Self-Attention (star)
Multi-head Self-attention allows the model to focus on different parts of the input sequence by extending the Self-attention to multiple “heads”, each of which learns a different subspace representation.
Why do we use Multi-head Self-Attention?

Capture different features

Different heads can learn different subspace representations of the input sequence, thus improving the expressive power of the model.

Focus on different positions

Each head can focus on different positional relationships in the input sequence (short distance dependence, long distance dependence, etc.).

Reduced dimensionality computation

Each head computes in lower dimensions, which can reduce computational complexity while avoiding too sparse distribution of attention in a single high-dimensional space.



Multi-head Self-Attention Structure



Query, Key and Value
Given the sequence \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}\) (\(n\): sequence length, \(d\): vector dimension), we should construct the independent query, key and value for each head. \(h=2\) heads shown in follows:



Two-head self-attention


For each head \(i\), we can define the corresponding weight matrix.
Query weight matrix: \(W^i_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_k}\)
Key weight matrix: \(W^i_K \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_k}\)
Value weight matrix: \(W^i_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_k}\)
So, we can get \(Q^i, K^i, V^i\) by these matrices.
\[
\begin{align*}
    Q^i &= A W^i_Q, \\
    K^i &= A W^i_K, \\
    V^i &= A W^i_V
\end{align*}
\]


Outputs Matrix
The method of calculation is the same as for single-head self-attention.
\[
\begin{align*}
    \text{Attention}(Q^i, K^i, V^i) &= \text{Softmax} \left( \frac{Q^i (K^i)^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}  \right) V^i
\end{align*}
\]
We can obtain the output \(B^i \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}\).
We concatenate \(h\) head into a matrix \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\): \[
\begin{align*}
    B &= \text{Concat} \left( Z^1, Z^2,...,Z^h  \right)
\end{align*}
\]
In the end, we should use a linear transformation to produce \(d\) dimension by \(B\). The formula is as follows: \[
\begin{align*}
    Output &= Z W_O
\end{align*}
\]
where \(W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) is weight matrix.

title: Self-Attention
text:
Positional Encoding
Why do we need Positional Encoding?
Self-attention is the global context-based mechanism that ignores the sequential information of the input sequence. For example, given the input sequence \([x_1, x_2, x_3]\) and \([x_3, x_1, x_2]\) without explicit positional information, the model will assume they are the same.

Solution
We set a vector for each vector, called position vector, donated as \(e^i\), and \(i\) shows the position. We can introduce a method in here.
Positional Encoding (\(PE\)) in Transformer is a fixed, sine and cosine function based approach. The core idea is to generate a vector for each position in the sequence, with sine wave information of different frequencies encoded in different dimensions of the vector. The formula is as follows:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \text{PE}(pos, 2i) &= \text{sin} \left( \frac{pos}{10000^\frac{2i}{d}}  \right), \\
    \text{PE}(pos, 2i+1) &= \text{cos} \left( \frac{pos}{10000^\frac{2i}{d}}  \right)
\end{align*}
\]
where \(pos\) is the position of the element in the sequence, \(i\) is the dimension index and \(d\) is the total dimension of the encoding vector.
Positional Encoding with input vectors X are added or spliced, and a common operation is direct addition:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \text{Input\_with\_Positional\_Encoding} &= X + PE
\end{align*}
\]

title: Self-Attention
text:
Self-attention for Speech
For a speech task, the length of the sequence usually reaches thousands of vectors, which will produces too large attention matrices. So, how can we reduce the computing complexity?

Truncated Self-Attention
We will introduce Truncated Self-Attention in here. It’s a improvement of self-attention that can reduce the computing complexity and retain the context information.
The core idea of the truncated self-attention is to limit the scope of the attentional computation.

title: Self-Attention
text:
Self-attention for Image
Images are two-dimensional structured data, unlike one-dimensional sequences in natural language. In order to apply self-attention on images, it is necessary to first perform appropriate preprocessing on images, which mainly includes the following two ways:

Directly based on the pixel matrix

The image pixels are directly spread into a one-dimensional sequence and then input into the self-attention mechanism

Patch-based slicing

Divide the image into several fixed-size patches (blocks), with each patch as an element in the sequence instead of each pixel as an element.

title: Self-Attention
text:
Self-attention VS XX

Self-attention VS CNN
In terms of computational nature, CNNs can be viewed as a localized, fixed-weight self-attention mechanism.

The sensory field corresponds to the range of attention

Self-attention can be computed over the global range of the input, and the feature update at each position depends on the features at all positions. It has an attention matrix dimension of \(n \times n\) (\(n\) is the number of pixels in the sequence or image).
The convolution operation of a CNN is localized, each time only in a fixed-size sensory field (e.g. \(3 \times 3\)) at a time.
CNN can be understood as a kind of localized attention, and the size of the receptive field is equivalent to limiting the scope of attention.

Weight sharing corresponds to the weight of attention

Self-attention’s weights are computed via the \(QK^T\) computationally obtained, is dynamically generated and reflects the similarity of the input data.
The weights of the CNN’s convolutional kernel are fixed and do not depend on the input data.
CNN can be understood as a special attention mechanism where the “attention weights” are fixed for the convolutional kernel and are not computed by similarity.


Self-attention VS RNN



Self-attention VS RNN


Where is “win”?

Self-attention can process all outputs in parallel, whereas RNNs must output them sequentially, making self-attention more efficient than RNNs
If you’re thinking about the vectors at the end of a sequence, you might need info about the vectors at the beginning of the sequence. If you’re using an RNN, you need to store the memory of processing the first vector all the way to the last vector. With self-attention, as long as you have a query and a key, you can directly compute.

Indexing and Slicing
To access an element based on its position relative to the end of the list, we can use negative indexing, like X[-1]. And we can access whole ranges of indices via slicing, like X[start:stop].

title: 2.1 Data Manipulation
text:
Operations
This part is for operating tensor. Among the most useful of mathematical operations are the elementwise operations. The common standard arithmetic operators for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and exponentiation can be upgraded to calculate the elements of any tensor with the same shape.


Code
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2, 4, 8])
y = torch.tensor([2, 2, 2, 2])
print(f"x + y is {x + y},\n x - y is {x-y},\n x * y is {x * y},\n x / y is {x / y},\n x ** y is {x ** y}")


x + y is tensor([ 3.,  4.,  6., 10.]),

 x ** y is tensor([ 1.,  4., 16., 64.])


We can also concatenate multiple tensors together to make a bigger tensor by cat.


Code
X = torch.arange(12, dtype=torch.float32).reshape((3,4))
Y = torch.tensor([[2.0, 1, 4, 3], [1, 2, 3, 4], [4, 3, 2, 1]])

#dim=0: [3,4], [3,4] -→ [6,4]
#dim=1: [3,4], [3,4] -→ [3,8]
torch.cat((X, Y), dim=1)
print(f"Shape of tensor after concatenating X and Y along the axis 0 is {torch.cat((X, Y), dim=0).shape}")
print(f"Shape of tensor after concatenating X and Y along the axis 1 is {torch.cat((X, Y), dim=1).shape}")

And summing all the elements in a tensor by X.sum().

title: 2.1 Data Manipulation
text:
Broadcasting
We can still perform elementwise binary operations on two tensors with different shape by invoking the broadcasting mechanism.
Its mechanism is as follows:

expand one or two arrays by copying the elements along axes with length 1 in order to make two tensors have the same shape.
perform an elementwise operation on the resulting arrays.



Code
a = torch.arange(3).reshape((3, 1))
b = torch.arange(2).reshape((1, 2))
print(f"Shape of tensor a is {a.shape} and tensor b is {b.shape}" )
print(f"Shape of a+b is {(a+b).shape}")


Shape of tensor a is torch.Size([3, 1]) and tensor b is torch.Size([1, 2])
Shape of a+b is torch.Size([3, 2])

title: 2.1 Data Manipulation
text:
Saving Memories
Runing operations can cause new memory to be allocated to host results.


Code
before = id(Y)
Y = Y+X
print(f"The address that previously stored Y was {before}, and the new address is {id(Y)} after the addition operation.")


The address that previously stored Y was 1995028788704, and the new address is 1995066453904 after the addition operation.


To save memory in case of unnecessary waste, we can operate directly on its original address. We can assign the result of an operation to a previously allocated array Y by using slice notation.


Code
Z = torch.zeros_like(Y)
before = id(Z)
print('id(Z):', id(Z))
Z[:] = X + Y
print(f"The address between the past and the present is the same: {before == id(Z)}")


id(Z): 1995065938544
The address between the past and the present is the same: True

text:
Exercise

Question 1
Run the code in this section. Change the conditional statement X == Y to X < Y or X > Y, and then see what kind of tensor you can get.

tensor([[[1., 1., 1.],

Reduction

x, x.sum()

A simple Function

x

In case of running out of memory, we should avoid allocating new memory every time we take a derivative.


Code
x.requires_grad_(True)
x.grad

# assign the function of x to y
y = 2 * torch.dot(x, x)
y


tensor(28., grad_fn=<MulBackward0>)


We can now take the gradient of \(y\) with respect to \(x\) by calling its backward method.


Code
y.backward()
x.grad


tensor([ 0.,  4.,  8., 12.])


The function \(y = 2 \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x}.\) with respect to \(x\) should be \(4x\). We can do a validation.


Code
x.grad == 4 *x


tensor([True, True, True, True])


Now, let’s calculate another function of \(x\) and take its gradient.


Code
x.grad.zero_() # set the gradient to 0
y = x.sum()
y.backward()
x.grad


tensor([1., 1., 1., 1.])

title: 2.5 Automatic Differentiation
text:
Backward for Non-Scalar Variables
When y is a vector, the derivative of \(y\) with respect to a vector \(x\) is a matrix called the Jacobian that contains the partial derivatives of each component of \(y\) with respect to each component of \(x\). Thus, the result of differentiation could be an even higher-order tensor.
For example, we often have a vector representing the value of our loss function calculated separately for each example among a batch of training example. Here, we just want to sum up the gradients computed individually for each example.


Code
#Calling backward on a non-scalar requires passing in a gradient argument that specifies the gradient of the differentiation function with respect to self.
x.grad.zero_()
y =x *x
y.backward(gradient=torch.ones(len(y)))
x.grad


tensor([0., 2., 4., 6.])

title: 2.5 Automatic Differentiation
text:
Detaching Computation
If we do not want to compute a gradient, we can detach the respective computational graph from the final result.
In the following example, we just want to focus on the direct influence of \(x\) on \(z\) rather than the influence conveyed via \(y\). We can create a new variable \(u\) that takes the same value as \(y\) whose provenance has been wiped out. Thus \(u\) has no ancestors in the graph and gradients do not flow through \(u\) to \(x\).


Code
x.grad.zero_()
y = x *x
u = y.detach()
z = u* x

z.sum().backward()
x.grad == u


tensor([True, True, True, True])


Thus, taking the gradient of \(z= x *u\) will yield the result \(u\). Also treat \(u\) as a constant instead of the partial derivative of \(z = x*x*x\) with respect to \(x\).
Since we record the computation results of \(y\), we can call the backward on \(y\), and get the gradient of \(y\) with respect to \(x\).


Code
x.grad.zero_()
y.sum().backward()
x.grad == 2*x


tensor([True, True, True, True])

import math

title: 3.1 Linear Regression
text:
Basics

Model
Supposed that our inputs consists of \(d\) features, we can assign each an index and express our prediction \(\hat{y}\)
\[
\hat{y} = w_1 x_1 + \cdots + w_d x_d + b.
\]
Collecting all features into a vector \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and all weights into a vector \(\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d\), we can express our model compactly via the dot product between \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(\mathbf{x}\):
\[
\hat{y} = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b.
\]
The vector \(\mathbf{x}\) corresponds to the feature of a single example. But we often have many samples in a batch. We can define it as the design matrix \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\). Here, \(\mathbf{X}\) contains one row for every example and one column for every feature. And we can express our model by:
\[
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{w} + b,
\]


Loss Function
Loss function quantify the distance between the real and predicted values of the target. We often minimize the loss when we train a model. For regression problems, the most common loss function is the squared error, which given by:
\[
l^{(i)}(\mathbf{w}, b) = \frac{1}{2} \left(\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)}\right)^2.
\]
And to measure the distance of a model on the entire dataset of \(n\) examples. we can define it as:
\[
L(\mathbf{w}, b) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n l^{(i)}(\mathbf{w}, b) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{2} \left(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b - y^{(i)}\right)^2.
\]
which \(\mathbf{w}^*, b^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}, b} L(\mathbf{w}, b).\)


Analytic Solution
Mathematically, we can find the minimum point of the loss plane by matrix derivation, and it can be defined as:
\[
\mathbf{w}^* = \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y}
\]


Minibatch Stochastic Gradient Descent
But the analytic solution is very restrictive on the problem, which prevents it from being widely used in deep learning. We can still train our model effectively if we cannot get the analytic solution by gradient descent.
The simplest use of gradient descent is to compute the loss function (the mean value of the loss for all the samples in the dataset) with respect to the derivatives of the model parameters. However, the implementation in practice can be very slow: because we have to traverse the whole dataset before each update of the parameters. Therefore, we usually take a small batch of random samples each time we need to compute an update, a variant of which is called minibatch stochastic gradient descent.
We can express the update as follows:
\[
(\mathbf{w}, b) \leftarrow (\mathbf{w}, b) - \frac{\eta}{|\mathcal{B}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}_t} \partial_{(\mathbf{w}, b)} l^{(i)}(\mathbf{w}, b).
\]
where \(\mathcal{B}_t\) means a minibatch.
In summary, minibatch SGD proceeds as follows: (1) initialize the values of the model parameters, typically at random; (2)iteratively sample random minibatches from the data, updating the parameters in the direction of the negative gradient. For quadratic losses and affine transformations, this has a closed-form expansion:
\[
\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \frac{\eta}{|\mathcal{B}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}_t} \partial_{\mathbf{w}} l^{(i)}(\mathbf{w}, b) = \mathbf{w} - \frac{\eta}{|\mathcal{B}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}_t} \mathbf{x}^{(i)} \left( \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b - y^{(i)} \right)
\]
\[
b \leftarrow b - \frac{\eta}{|\mathcal{B}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}_t} \partial_b l^{(i)}(\mathbf{w}, b) = b - \frac{\eta}{|\mathcal{B}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}_t} \left( \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b - y^{(i)} \right)
\]
where \(|\mathcal{B}|\) means the number of samples in a minibatch (batch_size), \(\eta\) refers to learning rate. And both of them are assigned before training.
Now, we can train our model by features (\(x\)), loss function and minibatch SGD.

title: 3.1 Linear Regression
text:
Vectorization for Speed
When training our models, we typically want to process whole minibatches of examples simultaneously. Doing this efficiently requires that we vectorize the calculations and leverage fast linear algebra libraries rather than writing costly for-loops in Python.
To start, we instantiate two 10000-dimensional vectors containing all 1s. And we call time() to compare the running time.


Code
%matplotlib inline
import math
import time
import numpy as np
import torch
from d2l import torch as d2l

n = 10000
a = torch.ones([n])
b = torch.ones([n])


We define a timers.


Code
class Timer:  
    def __init__(self):
        self.times = []
        self.start()

    def start(self):
        self.tik = time.time()

    def stop(self):
        self.times.append(time.time() - self.tik)
        return self.times[-1]

    def avg(self):
        return sum(self.times) / len(self.times)

    def sum(self):
        return sum(self.times)

    def cumsum(self):
        return np.array(self.times).cumsum().tolist()


First we use for-loops.


Code
c = torch.zeros(n)
timer = Timer()
for i in range(n):
    c[i] = a[i] + b[i]
print(f'{timer.stop():.5f} sec')


0.06500 sec


Alternatively, we rely on the reloaded + operator to compute the elementwise sum.


Code
timer.start()
d = a + b
f'{timer.stop():.5f} sec'


'0.00000 sec'


Obviously, the second method is dramatically faster than the first. Vectorizing code often yields order-of-magnitude speedups.

title: 3.1 Linear Regression
section: The Normal Distribution and Squared Loss
text:
The Normal Distribution and Squared Loss
A normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) is given as:
\[
p(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(x - \mu)^2 \right).
\]


Code
def normal(x, mu, sigma):
    p = 1 / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi * sigma**2)
    return p * np.exp(-0.5 * (x - mu)**2 / sigma**2)


We can visualize the normal distributions.


Code
# Use NumPy again for visualization
x = np.arange(-7, 7, 0.01)

# Mean and standard deviation pairs
params = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (3, 1)]
d2l.plot(x, [normal(x, mu, sigma) for mu, sigma in params], xlabel='x',
         ylabel='p(x)', figsize=(4.5, 2.5),
         legend=[f'mean {mu}, std {sigma}' for mu, sigma in params])









Note that changing the mean corresponds to a shift along the \(x\)-axis, and increasing the variance spreads the distribution out, lowering its peak.
One way to motivate linear regression with squared loss is to assume that observations arise from noisy measurements, where the noise \(\epsilon\) follows the normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\):
\[
y = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b + \epsilon \quad \text{where} \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).
\]
where \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\).
Thus, we can write out the likelihood of seeing a particular \(y\) for a given \(x\) via:
\[
P(y | \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \left( y - \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} - b \right)^2 \right).
\]
Based on the principle of maximum likelihood, the best values of parameters \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(b\) are those that maximize the likelihood of the entire dataset:
\[
P(y | \mathbf{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(y^{(i)} | \mathbf{x}^{(i)}).
\]
For historical reasons, optimizations are more often expressed as minimization rather than maximization. So, without changing anything, we can minimize the negative log-likelihood, which we can express as follows:
\[
- \log P(y | \mathbf{X}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{2} \log(2 \pi \sigma^2) + \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \left( y^{(i)} - \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} - b \right)^2.
\]
It follows that minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) is equivalent to the maximum likelihood estimation of a linear model under the assumption of additive Gaussian noise.

title: 3.5 Weight Decaying
text:
The most widely used technique for regularizing parametric machine learning models is Weight Decay, also called \(L_2\) regularization. We can measure the complexity of a function by the distance of its parameter from zero.
Our loss for linear regression was given by:
\[
L(\mathbf{w}, b) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{2} \left( \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b - y^{(i)} \right)^2.
\]
To penalize the size of the weight vector, we must somehow add \(||\mathbf{w}||^2\) to loss function. In practice, we characterize this penalty via the regularization constant \(\lambda\), and a nonnegative hyperparameter that we fit using validation data:
\[
L(\mathbf{w}, b) + \frac{\lambda}{2} \|\mathbf{w}\|^2.
\]


One reason for using \(L_2\) norm is that it imposes a large penalty on large components of the weight vector. This biases our learning algorithms toward models whose weights are distributed uniformly over a large number of features. In practice, this may make them more stable to observation errors in a single variable.
In contrast, the \(L_1\) norm causes the model to concentrate weights on a small component of feature, and clearing other weights to zero.
Minibatch stochastic gradient descent updates for \(L_2\)-regularized regression as follows:
\[
\mathbf{w} \leftarrow (1 - \eta \lambda) \mathbf{w} - \frac{\eta}{|\mathcal{B}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} \mathbf{x}^{(i)} \left( \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b - y^{(i)} \right).
\]

Implementation from Scratch

# L2-norm Penalty
def l2_penalty(w):
    return (w ** 2).sum() / 2



Initialize Model


Code
def init_params():
    w = torch.normal(0, 1, size=(num_inputs, 1), requires_grad=True)
    b = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)
    return [w, b]




Training


Code
def train(lambd):
    w, b = init_params()
    net, loss = lambda X: d2l.linreg(X, w, b), d2l.squared_loss
    num_epochs, lr = 100, 0.003
    animator = d2l.Animator(xlabel='epochs', ylabel='loss', yscale='log',
                            xlim=[5, num_epochs], legend=['train', 'test'])
    for epoch in range(num_epochs):
        for X, y in train_iter:
            l = loss(net(X), y) + lambd * l2_penalty(w) # add a l2-norm penalty
            l.sum().backward()
            d2l.sgd([w, b], lr, batch_size)
        if (epoch + 1) % 5 == 0:
            animator.add(epoch + 1, (d2l.evaluate_loss(net, train_iter, loss),
                                     d2l.evaluate_loss(net, test_iter, loss)))
    print('l2-norm of w：', torch.norm(w).item())

def train_concise(wd):
    net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(num_inputs, 1))
    for param in net.parameters():
        param.data.normal_()
    loss = nn.MSELoss(reduction='none')
    num_epochs, lr = 100, 0.003
    trainer = torch.optim.SGD([
        {"params":net[0].weight,'weight_decay': wd},
        {"params":net[0].bias}], lr=lr)
    animator = d2l.Animator(xlabel='epochs', ylabel='loss', yscale='log',
                            xlim=[5, num_epochs], legend=['train', 'test'])
    for epoch in range(num_epochs):
        for X, y in train_iter:
            trainer.zero_grad()
            l = loss(net(X), y)
            l.mean().backward()
            trainer.step()
        if (epoch + 1) % 5 == 0:
            animator.add(epoch + 1,
                         (d2l.evaluate_loss(net, train_iter, loss),
                          d2l.evaluate_loss(net, test_iter, loss)))
    print('l2-norm of w：', net[0].weight.norm().item())

The Softmax

Code
def softmax(X):
    X_exp = torch.exp(X)
    partition = X_exp.sum(1, keepdims = True)
    return X_exp / partition

text:
Training


Code
def trainer(train_iter, test_iter, model):

    #optimization algorithm (Adam). 
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001) # lr=0.001 default
    n_epochs= 10

    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        model.train()
        epoch_start_time = time.time()
        loss_record = []
        train_acc = 0.0
        #x: features, y: labels
        for X, y in train_iter:
            optimizer.zero_grad()               # Set gradient to zero.
            train_pred = model(X)  
            batch_loss = cross_entropy(train_pred, y)
            batch_loss.backward()               # Compute gradient(back propagation).
            optimizer.step()                    # Update parameters.
            train_acc += np.sum(np.argmax(train_pred.detach().cpu().numpy(), axis=1) == y.cpu().numpy())
            loss_record.append(batch_loss.detach().item()) #detach(): separation gradient

        mean_train_loss = sum(loss_record)/len(loss_record)
        train_acc = train_acc / len(mnist_train)

        model.eval() # Set our model to evaluation mode.
        loss_record = []
        test_acc = 0.0
        with torch.no_grad():
            for x, y in test_iter:
                test_pred = model(x)
                batch_loss = cross_entropy(test_pred, y)
                test_acc += np.sum(np.argmax(test_pred.detach().cpu().numpy(), axis=1) == y.cpu().numpy())
                loss_record.append(batch_loss.item())
            
            mean_test_loss = sum(loss_record)/len(loss_record)
            test_acc = test_acc / len(mnist_test)
            print('[%03d/%03d] %2.2f sec(s) Train Acc: %3.6f Loss: %3.6f | Test Acc: %3.6f loss: %3.6f' % \
              (epoch + 1, n_epochs, time.time() - epoch_start_time, \
               train_acc, mean_train_loss, test_acc, mean_test_loss))

title: 11.2 Attention Pooling by Similarity
text:
The Basic Theory of Self-attention please see here
In traditional pooling (e.g., Maximum Pooling, Average Pooling), the contributions of all features are usually equal or selected based on local regions (e.g., 3x3 or 2x2 windows). However, in Attention Pooling by Similarity, the weights of the pooling process are dynamically determined by the similarity between features. Specifically, features with higher similarity are given greater weights, while features with lower similarity are given smaller weights.
We have some common kernels:
\[
\alpha(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}) =
\begin{cases}
    \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{k}\|^2\right), & \text{Gaussian}; \\
    1 \text{ if } \|\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{k}\| \leq 1, & \text{Boxcar}; \\
    \max(0, 1 - \|\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{k}\|), & \text{Epanechnikov}.
\end{cases}
\]
We import all the packages we need in here.


Code
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn import functional as F
from d2l import torch as d2l

title: 11.2 Attention Pooling by Similarity
text:
Kernels and Data
First, we define some common kernels.


Code
# Define some kernels
def gaussian(x):
    return torch.exp(-x**2 / 2)

def boxcar(x):
    return torch.abs(x) < 1.0

def constant(x):
    return 1.0 + 0 * x

def epanechikov(x):
    return torch.max(1 - torch.abs(x), torch.zeros_like(x))

fig, axes = d2l.plt.subplots(1, 4, sharey=True, figsize=(12, 3))

kernels = (gaussian, boxcar, constant, epanechikov)
names = ('Gaussian', 'Boxcar', 'Constant', 'Epanechikov')
x = torch.arange(-2.5, 2.5, 0.1)
for kernel, name, ax in zip(kernels, names, axes):
    ax.plot(x.detach().numpy(), kernel(x).detach().numpy())
    ax.set_xlabel(name)

d2l.plt.show()









To see Nadaraya–Watson estimation in action, let’s define some training data. In the following we use the dependency
\[
y_i = 2\sin(x_i) + x_i^{0.8} + \epsilon,
\]

#Creat training dataset
n_train = 50 
x_train, _ = torch.sort(torch.rand(n_train) * 5) 

def f(x):
    return 2 * torch.sin(x) + x**0.8

y_train = f(x_train) + torch.normal(0.0, 0.5, (n_train,))
x_test = torch.arange(0, 5, 0.1) 
y_truth = f(x_test)  
n_test = len(x_test)

title: 11.2 Attention Pooling by Similarity
text:
Attention Pooling via Nadaraya–Watson Regression
Now that we have data and kernels, all we need is a function that computes the kernel regression estimates. Note that we also want to obtain the relative kernel weights in order to perform some minor diagnostics. Hence we first compute the kernel between all training features (covariates) \(x_train\) and all validation features \(x_val\). This yields a matrix, which we subsequently normalize. When multiplied with the training labels \(y_train\) we obtain the estimates. The normalized relative kernel weights (\(attention\_w\) below) are the attention weights.


Code
#y_hat: pred, attention_w: attention weight
def nadaraya_watson(x_train, y_train, x_val, kernel):
    dists = x_train.reshape((-1, 1)) - x_val.reshape((1, -1)) #dist between train and valid
    # Each column/row corresponds to each query/key
    k = kernel(dists).type(torch.float32)
    # Normalization over keys for each query
    attention_w = k / k.sum(0)
    y_hat = y_train@attention_w
    return y_hat, attention_w


The whole calculation is as follows:
\[
f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{K(x - x_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^n K(x - x_j)} y_i,
\]
where \(K\) is the kernel.
And it has a more common formula:
\[
f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha(x, x_i) y_i,
\]
where \(x\) is the query, \([x_i, y_i]\) is the key-value pair.
Let’s have a look at the kind of estimates that the different kernels produce.


Code
def plot_kernel_reg(y_hat):
    d2l.plot(x_test, [y_truth, y_hat], 'x', 'y', legend=['Truth', 'Pred'],
             xlim=[0, 5], ylim=[-1, 5])
    d2l.plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'o', alpha=0.5)



Constant kernel

The estimator calculates the average of all training sample output values based on average convergence.


Code
y_hat, attention_w_constant = nadaraya_watson(x_train, y_train, x_test, kernel= constant)
plot_kernel_reg(y_hat)









From the results, it is not the model we need.

Gaussian kernel



Code
y_hat, attention_w_Gaussian = nadaraya_watson(x_train, y_train, x_test, kernel= gaussian)
plot_kernel_reg(y_hat)










Boxcar kernel



Code
y_hat, attention_w_Boxcar = nadaraya_watson(x_train, y_train, x_test, kernel= boxcar)
plot_kernel_reg(y_hat)










Epanechikov



Code
y_hat, attention_w_Epanechikov = nadaraya_watson(x_train, y_train, x_test, kernel= epanechikov)
plot_kernel_reg(y_hat)









Let’s see their attention maps.


Code
def plot(attention_w, names):
    fig, axes = d2l.plt.subplots(1, 4, sharey=True, figsize=(12, 3))
    for name, attention, ax in zip(names, attention_w, axes):
        pcm = ax.imshow(attention.detach().numpy(), cmap='Reds')
        ax.set_xlabel(name)
    fig.colorbar(pcm, ax=axes, shrink=0.7)

attention_w = [attention_w_Gaussian, attention_w_Boxcar, attention_w_constant, attention_w_Epanechikov] 
plot(attention_w, names)









The visualization clearly shows why the estimates for Gaussian, Boxcar, and Epanechikov are very similar: after all, they are derived from very similar attention weights, despite the different functional form of the kernel.

title: 5.1 Multilayer Perceptrons
text:
Linear models often fail in real-world scenarios. For example, the decrease of body temperature does not reduce risk. Although we can determine the risk based on the distance to the normal temperature, it is still not usable on the image classification when we faced an inverted cat/dog images remain in the same category. And linear models fail to capture context-dependent relationships between the neighboring pixels.



We can overcome limitations of linear models by introducing nonlinearity through hidden layers. The easiest way to do this is to stack many fully connected layers on top of one another. Each layer feeds into the layer above it, until we generate outputs. This architecture is commonly called a multilayer perceptron, often abbreviated as MLP.
\[
\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{W}^{(1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}, \\
\mathbf{O} = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{W}^{(2)} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}.
\]

\(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) is a minibatch of \(n\) examples where each example has \(d\) inputs.
\(\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times h}\) is the outputs of the hidden layer, which are hidden representations.
\(\mathbf{W}^{(1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times h}\) is hidden layer weights, and \(\mathbf{b}^{(1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times h}\) is biases.
\(\mathbf{W}^{(2)} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times q}\) is output-layer weights, and \(\mathbf{b}^{(2)} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times q}\) is biases.

In order to realize the potential of multilayer architectures, we need more key ingredient: a nonlinear activation function \(\sigma\) to be applied to each hidden unit. The formula is as follows:
\[
\mathbf{H} = \sigma(\mathbf{X} \mathbf{W}^{(1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}), \\
\mathbf{O} = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{W}^{(2)} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)},
\]

\mathbf{H} = \sigma(\mathbf{X} \mathbf{W}^{(1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}), \\
\mathbf{O} = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{W}^{(2)} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)},
\]

title: 5.1 Multilayer Perceptrons
text:
Activation Functions

ReLU Function
\[
\mathrm{ReLU}(x) = \max(x, 0).
\]


Code
import torch
from d2l import torch as d2l

x = torch.arange(-8.0, 8.0, 0.1, requires_grad=True)
y = torch.relu(x)
d2l.plot(x.detach(), y.detach(), 'x', 'relu(x)', figsize=(5, 2.5))









The reason for using ReLU is that its derivatives are particularly well behaved: either they vanish or they just let the argument through. This makes optimization better behaved and it mitigated the well-documented problem of vanishing gradients that plagued previous versions of neural networks.


Code
y.backward(torch.ones_like(x), retain_graph=True)
d2l.plot(x.detach(), x.grad, 'x', 'grad of relu', figsize=(5, 2.5))











Sigmoid Function
\[
\text{sigmoid}(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-x)}.
\]


Code
y = torch.sigmoid(x)
d2l.plot(x.detach(), y.detach(), 'x', 'sigmoid(x)', figsize=(5, 2.5))









function is a smooth, differentiable approximation of the threshold cell. The sigmoid function is still widely used as an activation function on output units when we want to treat the output as the probability of a binary classification problem.


Code
x.grad.data.zero_()
y.backward(torch.ones_like(x),retain_graph=True)
d2l.plot(x.detach(), x.grad, 'x', 'grad of sigmoid', figsize=(5, 2.5))











tanh Function
\[
\tanh(x) = \frac{1 - \exp(-2x)}{1 + \exp(-2x)}.
\]


Code

d2l.plot(x.detach(), y.detach(), 'x', 'tanh(x)', figsize=(5, 2.5))

y.backward(torch.ones_like(x),retain_graph=True)
d2l.plot(x.detach(), x.grad, 'x', 'grad of tanh', figsize=(5, 2.5))

Code
import torch
import torchvision
from torch.utils import data
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from torch import nn
from torchvision import transforms
from d2l import torch as d2l
import time
import numpy as np

d2l.use_svg_display()




To begin, we will implement an MLP with one hidden layer and 256 hidden units. Both the number of layers and their width are adjustable
Notably, we typically choose the layer widths to be divisible by larger powers of 2. This is computationally efficient due to the way memory is allocated and addressed in hardware.
Again, we will represent our parameters with several tensors. Note that for every layer, we must keep track of one weight matrix and one bias vector. As always, we allocate memory for the gradients of the loss with respect to these parameters.


Code
# Activate Function
def relu(X):
    a = torch.zeros_like(X)
    return torch.max(X, a)

class MLPScratch(d2l.Classifier):
    def __init__(self, num_inputs, num_outputs, num_hiddens, sigma=0.01):
        super().__init__()
        self.save_hyperparameters()
        self.W1 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(num_inputs, num_hiddens) * sigma)
        self.b1 = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(num_hiddens))
        self.W2 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(num_hiddens, num_outputs) * sigma)
        self.b2 = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(num_outputs))
    
    def forward(self, X):
        X = X.reshape((-1, self.num_inputs))
        H = relu(torch.matmul(X, self.W1) + self.b1)
        return torch.matmul(H, self.W2) + self.b2







Code
trans = transforms.ToTensor()
mnist_train = torchvision.datasets.FashionMNIST(root="./data", train=True, transform=trans, download = True)
mnist_test = torchvision.datasets.FashionMNIST(root="./data", train=False, transform=trans, download = True)

batch_size = 256

train_iter = DataLoader(mnist_train, batch_size, shuffle= True)
test_iter = DataLoader(mnist_test, batch_size)







Code
def trainer_scratch(train_iter, test_iter, model):

    #optimization algorithm (Adam). 
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001) # lr=0.001 default
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

    n_epochs= 10

    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        model.train()
        epoch_start_time = time.time()
        loss_record = []
        train_acc = 0.0
        #x: features, y: labels
        for X, y in train_iter:
            optimizer.zero_grad()               # Set gradient to zero.
            train_pred = model(X)  
            batch_loss = criterion(train_pred, y)
            batch_loss.backward()               # Compute gradient(back propagation).
            optimizer.step()                    # Update parameters.
            train_acc += np.sum(np.argmax(train_pred.detach().cpu().numpy(), axis=1) == y.cpu().numpy())
            loss_record.append(batch_loss.detach().item()) #detach(): separation gradient

        mean_train_loss = sum(loss_record)/len(loss_record)
        train_acc = train_acc / len(mnist_train)

        model.eval() # Set our model to evaluation mode.
        loss_record = []
        test_acc = 0.0
        with torch.no_grad():
            for x, y in test_iter:
                test_pred = model(x)
                batch_loss = criterion(test_pred, y)
                test_acc += np.sum(np.argmax(test_pred.detach().cpu().numpy(), axis=1) == y.cpu().numpy())
                loss_record.append(batch_loss.item())
            
            mean_test_loss = sum(loss_record)/len(loss_record)
            test_acc = test_acc / len(mnist_test)
            print('[%03d/%03d] %2.2f sec(s) Train Acc: %3.6f Loss: %3.6f | Test Acc: %3.6f loss: %3.6f' % \
              (epoch + 1, n_epochs, time.time() - epoch_start_time, \
               train_acc, mean_train_loss, test_acc, mean_test_loss))

model = MLPScratch(num_inputs=784, num_outputs=10, num_hiddens=256)
trainer_scratch(train_iter, test_iter, model)

title: 5.4 Numerical Stability
text:
Vanishing Gradients
During backpropagation, gradients become increasingly smaller as they propagate through deeper layers, causing shallow layers to update very slowly or stop learning effectively.

Accumulation in Chain Rule
During backpropagation, gradients are multiplied layer by layer through the chain rule. If the product of weights or activation derivatives is consistently less than 1 (e.g., in Sigmoid), gradients shrink exponentially (vanishing).


Visualization
Let’s take a closer look at the sigmoid to see why it can cause vanishing gradients.


Code
x = torch.arange(-8.0, 8.0, 0.1, requires_grad=True)
y = torch.sigmoid(x)
y.backward(torch.ones_like(x))

d2l.plot(x.detach().numpy(), [y.detach().numpy(), x.grad.numpy()],
         legend=['sigmoid', 'gradient'], figsize=(4.5, 2.5))









As you can see, the sigmoid’s gradient vanishes both when its inputs are large and when they are small. Moreover, when backpropagating through many layers, unless we are in the Goldilocks zone, where the inputs to many of the sigmoids are close to zero, the gradients of the overall product may vanish.


Solution

Change Sigmoid function to ReLU function
Weight Initialization
Batch Normalization
Using shallower network …

title: 5.4 Numerical Stability
text:
Exploding Gradients
Contrary to the vanishing gradients, gradients grow exponentially as they propagate backward through the network, leading to excessively large updates to the model parameters and unstable training.

Accumulation in Chain Rule
During backpropagation, gradients are multiplied layer by layer through the chain rule. If the product of weights or activation derivatives is consistently greater than 1, gradients grow exponentially (exploding).


Visualization
To illustrate this a bit better, we draw 100 Gaussian random matrices and multiply them with some initial matrix.

print('a single matrix \n',M)
for i in range(100):

title: 6. Builders’ Guide
text:
We can regard a module as a single layer, a component consisting of multiple layers, to implement a complex network.



Multiple layers are combined into modules, forming repeating patterns of larger models




Code
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn import functional as F
from d2l import torch as d2l


Refers to the MLPs concise implement, we generates a network with one fully connected hidden layer with 256 units and ReLU activation, followed by a fully connected layer with ten units.


Code
net = nn.Sequential(nn.LazyLinear(256), nn.ReLU(), nn.LazyLinear(10))

X = torch.rand(2, 20)
net(X).shape


torch.Size([2, 10])




The basic functionality that each module must provide:

Ingest input data as arguments to its forward propagation method.
Generate an output by having the forward propagation method return a value. Note that the output may have a different shape from the input. For example, the first fully connected layer in our model above ingests an input of arbitrary dimension but returns an output of dimension 256.
Calculate the gradient of its output with respect to its input, which can be accessed via its backpropagation method. Typically this happens automatically.
Store and provide access to those parameters necessary for executing the forward propagation computation.
Initialize model parameters as needed.



Code
class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden = nn.LazyLinear(256) # [num, A] --> [num, 256]
        self.out = nn.LazyLinear(10)  # output: 10 dims
    
    def forward(self, X):
        print(f"Shape of hidden layers is {self.hidden(X).shape}")
        return self.out(F.relu(self.hidden(X)))

print(f"Shape of input is {X.shape}")
net = MLP()
net(X).shape


Shape of input is torch.Size([2, 20])
Shape of hidden layers is torch.Size([2, 256])


torch.Size([2, 10])





Recall that Sequential was designed to daisy-chain other modules together.


Code
class MySequential(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, *args):
        super().__init__()
        for idx, module in enumerate(args):
            self.add_module(str(idx), module)

    def forward(self, X):
        for module in self.children():
            X = module(X)
        return X

net = MySequential(nn.LazyLinear(256), nn.ReLU(), nn.LazyLinear(10))
net(X).shape


torch.Size([2, 10])





Sometimes we want to incorporate terms that are neither the result of previous layers nor updatable parameters. We call these constant parameters. So we implement a FixedHiddenMLP class as follows.


Code
class FixedHiddenMLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.rand_weight = torch.rand((20, 20))
        self.linear = nn.LazyLinear(20)
    
    def forward(self, X):
        X = self.linear(X)
        X = F.relu(torch.mm(X, self.rand_weight)+1)
        X = self.linear(X)

        while X.abs().sum() >1:
            X/=2
        return X.sum()


self.rand_weight is initialized randomly at instantiation and are thereafter constant. This weight is not a model parameter and thus it is never updated by backpropagation. The network then passes the output of this “fixed” layer through a fully connected layer.


Code
net = FixedHiddenMLP()
net(X)


tensor(0.0398, grad_fn=<SumBackward0>)


We can mix and match various ways of assembling modules together.


Code
class NestMLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.LazyLinear(64), nn.ReLU(),
                                nn.LazyLinear(32), nn.ReLU())
        self.linear = nn.LazyLinear(16)

    def forward(self, X):
        return self.linear(self.net(X))

# FixedHiddenMLP input: [num, 20]
chimera = nn.Sequential(NestMLP(), nn.LazyLinear(20), FixedHiddenMLP())
chimera(X)


tensor(0.1377, grad_fn=<SumBackward0>)

self.rand_weight is initialized randomly at instantiation and are thereafter constant. This weight is not a model parameter and thus it is never updated by backpropagation. The network then passes the output of this “fixed” layer through a fully connected layer.


Code
net = FixedHiddenMLP()
net(X)


tensor(0.0398, grad_fn=<SumBackward0>)


We can mix and match various ways of assembling modules together.


Code
class NestMLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.LazyLinear(64), nn.ReLU(),
                                nn.LazyLinear(32), nn.ReLU())
        self.linear = nn.LazyLinear(16)

    def forward(self, X):
        return self.linear(self.net(X))

# FixedHiddenMLP input: [num, 20]
chimera = nn.Sequential(NestMLP(), nn.LazyLinear(20), FixedHiddenMLP())
chimera(X)


tensor(0.1377, grad_fn=<SumBackward0>)

title: 6. Builders’ Guide
text:
Tied Parameters
We often share parameters across multiple layers. In the following, we allocate a fully connected layer and then use its parameters specifically to set those of another layer.


Code
shared = nn.LazyLinear(8)
net = nn.Sequential(nn.LazyLinear(8), nn.ReLU(),
                    shared, nn.ReLU(),
                    shared, nn.ReLU(),
                    nn.LazyLinear(1))
print(f"the structure of net is\n {net}")
net(X)
print(net[2].weight.data[0] == net[4].weight.data[0])
net[2].weight.data[0, 0] = 100
print(net[2].weight.data[0] == net[4].weight.data[0])


the structure of net is
 Sequential(

  (1): ReLU()
  (2): LazyLinear(in_features=0, out_features=8, bias=True)
  (3): ReLU()
  (4): LazyLinear(in_features=0, out_features=8, bias=True)
  (5): ReLU()
  (6): LazyLinear(in_features=0, out_features=1, bias=True)
)

text:
Built-in Initialization
The code below initializes all weight parameter as Gaussian random variables with standard deviation 0.01, while bias parameters are cleared to zero.


Code
def init_normal_1(module):
    if type(module) == nn.Linear:
        nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0, std=0.01)
        nn.init.zeros_(module.bias)

net.apply(init_normal_1)
net[0].weight.data[0], net[0].bias.data[0]

We can also initialize all the parameters to a given constant value.

net.apply(init_normal_2)

title: 6. Builders’ Guide
text:
Lazy Initialization
So far, it might seem that we got away with being sloppy in setting up our networks Specifically, we did the following unintuitive things, which might not seem like they should work:

We defined the network architectures without specifying the input dimensionality.
We added layers without specifying the output dimension of the previous layer.
We even “initialized” these parameters before providing enough information to determine how many parameters our models should contain.

We introduce the defers initialization in here, which can wait until the first time we pass data through the model, to infer the sizes of each layer on the fly.
To begin, let’s initialize an MLP.


Code
net = nn.Sequential(nn.LazyLinear(256), nn.ReLU(), nn.LazyLinear(10))


Since the input dimension remains unknown, the network cannot possibly know the dimensions of the input layer’s weights.
The framework has not yet initialized any parameters. We confirm by attempting to access the parameters below.


Code
net[0].weight


<UninitializedParameter>


Next let’s pass data through the network to make the framework finally initialize parameters.


Code
X = torch.rand(2, 20)
net(X)

net[0].weight.shape


torch.Size([256, 20])

title: 6. Builders’ Guide
text:
Layers without Parameters
To start, we construct a custom layer that does not have any parameters of its own and feed some data through it.


Code
class CenteredLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def forward(self, X):
        return X - X.mean()

layer = CenteredLayer()
layer(torch.tensor([1.0, 2, 3, 4, 5]))


tensor([-2., -1.,  0.,  1.,  2.])


Next, we can incorporate our layers as a component in constructing more complex models.


Code
net = nn.Sequential(nn.LazyLinear(128), CenteredLayer())


As an extra sanity check, we can send random data through the network and check that the mean is in fact 0.


Code
Y = net(torch.rand(4, 8))
Y.mean()


tensor(3.2596e-09, grad_fn=<MeanBackward0>)


Because we are dealing with floating point numbers, we may still see a very small nonzero number due to quantization.

title: 6. Builders’ Guide
text:
Layers with Parameters
Now let’s implement our own version of the fully connected layer. Recall that this layer requires two parameters, one to represent the weight and the other for the bias.


Code
class MyLinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, out_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(in_dim, out_dim))
        self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(out_dim,))
    def forward(self, X):
        linear = torch.matmul(X, self.weight.data) + self.bias.data
        return F.relu(linear)

model = MyLinear(5, 3)
model.weight


Parameter containing:
tensor([[ 1.0759, -1.3369,  1.7752],
        [ 0.5968, -1.5477, -1.2598],
        [ 0.0623,  0.3213,  0.5407],
        [-1.1469,  0.1192,  0.8214],
        [ 1.0849,  1.3784, -1.0405]], requires_grad=True)


We can directly carry out forward propagation calculations using custom layers.


Code
model(torch.rand(2, 5))


tensor([[0.2310, 0.0000, 0.2028],
        [0.9659, 0.0000, 1.7983]])


We can also construct models using custom layers. Once we have that we can use it just like the built-in fully connected layer.


Code
model = nn.Sequential(MyLinear(64, 8), MyLinear(8, 1))
model(torch.rand(2, 64))


tensor([[0.0000],
        [3.0537]])

title: 6. Builders’ Guide
text:
Loading and Saving Tensors
We can directly invoke the load and save functions to read and write them respectively. Both functions require that we supply a name, and save requires as input the variable to be saved.


Code
x = torch.arange(4)
torch.save(x, 'x-file')

#read data
x2 = torch.load('x-file', weights_only=True)
x2


tensor([0, 1, 2, 3])


We can store a list of tensors and then read them back into memory.


Code
y = torch.zeros(4)
torch.save([x, y],'x-files')
x2, y2 = torch.load('x-files')
(x2, y2)

We recommend you start setting `weights_only=True` for any use case where you don't have full control of the loaded file. Please open an issue on GitHub for any issues related to this experimental feature.
  x2, y2 = torch.load('x-files')


(tensor([0, 1, 2, 3]), tensor([0., 0., 0., 0.]))


We can even write and read a dictionary that maps from strings to tensors. This is convenient when we want to read or write all the weights in a model.


Code
mydict = {'x': x, 'y': y}
torch.save(mydict, 'mydict')
mydict2 = torch.load('mydict', weights_only=True)
mydict2


{'x': tensor([0, 1, 2, 3]), 'y': tensor([0., 0., 0., 0.])}

title: 6. Builders’ Guide
text:
Loading and Saving Model Parameters
The deep learning framework provides built-in functionalities to load and save entire networks. Let’s start with our familiar MLP.


Code
class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden = nn.LazyLinear(256)
        self.output = nn.LazyLinear(10)
    def forward(self, X):
        return self.output(F.relu(self.hidden(X)))

net = MLP()
X = torch.randn(size= (2,20))
Y= net(X)


Next, we store the parameters of the model as a file with the name “mlp.params”.


Code
torch.save(net.state_dict(), './data/mlp.params')


To recover the model, we instantiate a clone of the original MLP model. Instead of randomly initializing the model parameters, we read the parameters stored in the file directly.


Code
clone = MLP()
clone.load_state_dict(torch.load('./data/mlp.params', weights_only=True))
clone.eval()


MLP(
  (hidden): LazyLinear(in_features=0, out_features=256, bias=True)
  (output): LazyLinear(in_features=0, out_features=10, bias=True)
)

title: 6. Builders’ Guide
6. Builders’ Guide
text:
Tensors and GPUs
By default, tensors are created on the CPU. We can query the device where the tensor is located.


Code
x = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3])
x.device


device(type='cpu')



Storage on the GPU
we can specify a storage device when creating a tensor. Next, we create the tensor variable X on the first gpu.


Code
X = torch.ones(2, 3, device=try_gpu())
X


tensor([[1., 1., 1.],
        [1., 1., 1.]], device='cuda:0')




Copying
If we want to compute X + Y, we need to decide where to perform this operation. Do not simply add X and Y, since this will result in an exception. The runtime engine would not know what to do: it cannot find data on the same device and it fails. Since Y lives on the second GPU, we need to move X there before we can add the two.

title: 6. Builders’ Guide
text:
Neural Networks and GPUs
Similarly, a neural network model can specify devices. The following code puts the model parameters on the GPU.


Code
net = nn.Sequential(nn.LazyLinear(1))
net = net.to(device=try_gpu())
net(X)


tensor([[-0.5242],
        [-0.5242]], device='cuda:0', grad_fn=<AddmmBackward0>)


Let’s confirm that the model parameters are stored on the same GPU.


Code
net[0].weight.data.device


device(type='cuda', index=0)

   exit 1
fi

#check-failure.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash

file="failure.sh"
success_count=0

while true; do
    ((success_count++))
    # stdout to run.log, stderr to error.log
    ./$file >> run.log 2>> error.log
    if [[ $? -eq 1 ]]; then
        echo "The script failed after $success_count runs."
        echo "Captured standard error:"
        cat error.log
        break
    fi
done

Dataset
We can download data from MNIST
Some basic information about the dataset:

datafile = os.path.join('recognize_handwritten','data','MNIST.mat')
minst_data = scio.loadmat(datafile)

label = torch.Tensor(minst_data['gnd'])

Therefore, the shape of data is 700000×785 consisting of \(28 × 28 pixels + 1 label\),
Since the dataset doesn’t make a distinction between the test_data and the train_data, we’ll have to divide them manually.


Code
def data_split(data_set, ratio, seed):
    split_1_size = int(ratio * len(data_set)) 
    split_2_size = len(data_set) - split_1_size
    split_2_set, split_1_set = random_split(data_set, [split_2_size, split_1_size], generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed))
    #Proportionally divide split1, the rest is split2
    return np.array(split_2_set), np.array(split_1_set)

train_data, test_data = data_split(minst_data, config['test_ratio'], config['seed'])

print("Shape of train_data is {}".format(train_data.shape))
print("Shape of test_data is {}".format(test_data.shape))

We processed the dataset into labels with image pixel values.

# extract 784 columns
train_images, valid_images, test_images =train_data[:, :-1], valid_data[:, :-1], test_data[:, :-1]
# extract the last column
train_labels, valid_labels, test_labels =train_data[:, -1], valid_data[:, -1], test_data[:, -1]

print("the shape of train_images is {}".format(train_images.shape))


the shape of train_images is (52000, 1, 28, 28)


So, we’ve got three sets of data — train_data, valid_data, and test_data, and we’ve also got their features. Now, it’s time to construct our dataset.


Code
#x: Features.
#y: Targets, if none, do prediction.
class ImgDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, x, y=None, transform=None):
        self.x = torch.FloatTensor(x)
        if y is None:
            self.y = y
        else:
            self.y = torch.LongTensor(y)
        self.transform = transform
    def __getitem__(self, index):
        X = self.x[index]
        if self.transform is not None:
            X = self.transform(X)
        if self.y is not None:
            Y = self.y[index]
            return X, Y
        else:
            return X
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.x)

# Data Augmentation
# transform = transforms.Compose([
#     transforms.ToPILImage(),               # 将 NumPy 转为 PIL 图像
#     transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(),     # 随机水平翻转
#     transforms.RandomRotation(15),         # 随机旋转
#     transforms.ToTensor(),                 # 转为张量
#     transforms.Normalize([0.5], [0.5])     # 标准化
# ])

train_dataset, valid_dataset, test_dataset = ImgDataset(train_images, train_labels), \
                                            ImgDataset(valid_images, valid_labels), \
                                            ImgDataset(test_images)

train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=config['batch_size'], shuffle=True, pin_memory=True)
valid_loader = DataLoader(valid_dataset, batch_size=config['batch_size'], shuffle=True, pin_memory=True)
test_loader = DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size=config['batch_size'], shuffle=False, pin_memory=True)


At this point, we’ve finished building the dataset. With train_loader, we can get bulk data during the training process and pass it to the model. It’s time to construct our model.


Model
We adopt a network consisting of two convolutional layers and three fully connected layers. BatchNorm2d and Dropout can introduce the regularization into network, but it’s more redundant for the MINST dataset and also affects the training performance.


Code
class Classifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim):
        super(Classifier, self).__init__()
        self.layers = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(input_dim, 16, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1),  # [16, 28, 28]
            #nn.BatchNorm2d(16),  Regularization
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2),  # [16, 14, 14]

            nn.Conv2d(16, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1),  # [32, 14, 14]
            nn.ReLU(),

            nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1),  # [64, 14, 14]
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2),  # [64, 7, 7]

        )
        self.fc = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(64 * 7 * 7, 256),
            nn.ReLU(),
            #nn.Dropout(p=0.5), Regularization
            nn.Linear(256, 512),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(512, 10),
        )
#forward propagation
    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.layers(x)
        out = out.view(out.size()[0], -1) #Flattens the tensor to feed it into the fully connected layer.
        return self.fc(out)




Training Loop


Code
def trainer(train_loader, valid_loader, model, config, device):

    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()  # loss: CrossEntropyLoss
    #optimization algorithm (Adam). 
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=config['learning_rate']) 
    
    writer = SummaryWriter() # Writer of tensorboard.

    n_epochs, best_loss, step, early_stop_count = config['n_epochs'], math.inf, 0, 0

    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        model.train()
        epoch_start_time = time.time()
        loss_record = []
        train_acc = 0.0
        #x: features, y: labels
        for x, y in train_loader:
            optimizer.zero_grad()               # Set gradient to zero.
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)   # Move our data to device. 
            train_pred = model(x)  
            batch_loss = criterion(train_pred, y)
            batch_loss.backward()               # Compute gradient(back propagation).
            optimizer.step()                    # Update parameters.
            step += 1
            train_acc += np.sum(np.argmax(train_pred.detach().cpu().numpy(), axis=1) == y.cpu().numpy())
            loss_record.append(batch_loss.detach().item()) #detach(): separation gradient

        mean_train_loss = sum(loss_record)/len(loss_record)
        train_acc = train_acc / train_dataset.__len__()
        writer.add_scalar('Loss/train', mean_train_loss, step)
        writer.add_scalar('Accuracy/train', train_acc, step)

        model.eval() # Set our model to evaluation mode.
        loss_record = []
        valid_acc = 0.0
        with torch.no_grad():
            for x, y in valid_loader:
                x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
                valid_pred = model(x)
                batch_loss = criterion(valid_pred, y)
                valid_acc += np.sum(np.argmax(valid_pred.detach().cpu().numpy()
, axis=1) == y.cpu().numpy())
                loss_record.append(batch_loss.item())
            
            mean_valid_loss = sum(loss_record)/len(loss_record)
            valid_acc = valid_acc / valid_dataset.__len__()
            print('[%03d/%03d] %2.2f sec(s) Train Acc: %3.6f Loss: %3.6f | Val Acc: %3.6f loss: %3.6f' % \
              (epoch + 1, n_epochs, time.time() - epoch_start_time, \
               train_acc, mean_train_loss, valid_acc, mean_valid_loss))
            writer.add_scalar('Loss/valid', mean_valid_loss, step)
            writer.add_scalar('Accuracy/valid', valid_acc, step)

        if mean_valid_loss < best_loss:
            best_loss = mean_valid_loss
            torch.save(model.state_dict(), config['save_path']) # Save our best model
            print('Saving model with loss {:.3f}...'.format(best_loss))
            early_stop_count = 0
        else: 
            early_stop_count += 1

        if early_stop_count >= config['early_stop']:
            print('\nModel is not improving, so we halt the training session.')
            return

# Reversing the black and white thresholds for each pixel
def accessPiexl(img):
    height = img.shape[0]
    width = img.shape[1]
    for i in range(height):
       for j in range(width):
           img[i][j] = 255 - img[i][j]
    return img

# Inverse binarized image
def accessBinary(img, threshold=165):
    img = accessPiexl(img)
    kernel = np.ones((3, 3), np.uint8)
    img = cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (3, 3), 0) #Gaussian filter
    img = cv2.erode(img, kernel, iterations=1) #Border burr removal
    # adaptive filter
    img = cv2.adaptiveThreshold(img, 255, cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_MEAN_C, cv2.THRESH_BINARY, 7, -9)
    img = cv2.dilate(img, kernel, iterations=1)
    return img

# For showing prediction results
def showResults(path, borders, results=None):
    img = cv2.imread(path)
    for i, border in enumerate(borders):
        cv2.rectangle(img, border[0], border[1], (0, 0, 255))
        if results is not None:
            cv2.putText(img, str(results[i]), border[0], cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_COMPLEX, 0.8, (0, 255, 0), 1)
    cv2.waitKey(0)
    cv2.imwrite('recognize_handwritten/out.jpg',img)
    display(Image(filename='recognize_handwritten/out.jpg'))

#Search the edge, and return the top right and bottom left coner of the digits
def findBorderContours(path, maxArea=1800):
    img = cv2.imread(path, cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
    img = accessBinary(img)
    contours, hierarchy = cv2.findContours(img, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_NONE)
    borders = []
    for contour in contours:
        #creat a boder
        x, y, w, h = cv2.boundingRect(contour)
        if w*h > maxArea:
            #the coordinate of boder
            border = [(x, y), (x+w, y+h)]
            borders.append(border)
    return borders

def transUSPS(path, borders, size=(28, 28)):
    imgData = np.zeros((len(borders), size[0], size[0], 1), dtype='uint8')
    img = cv2.imread(path, cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
    img = accessBinary(img)
    for i, border in enumerate(borders):
        borderImg = img[border[0][1]:border[1][1], border[0][0]:border[1][0]]
        #Expand pixels based on maximum edge make the border close to square
        extendPiexl = (max(borderImg.shape) - min(borderImg.shape)) // 2
        #make border
        targetImg = cv2.copyMakeBorder(borderImg, 7, 7, extendPiexl + 7, extendPiexl + 7, cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT)
        targetImg = cv2.resize(targetImg, size)
        # expand dimension
        targetImg = np.expand_dims(targetImg, axis=-1)
        imgData[i] = targetImg
    return imgData

#get labels from .txt
def take_train_label(phoneme_path):
    label_dict = {}
    for line in open(os.path.join(phoneme_path, 'train_labels.txt')).readlines():
        line = line.strip('\n').split(' ') 
        label_dict[line[0]] = [int(p) for p in line[1:]]
    print(f"Length of labels is {len(label_dict)}")
    return label_dict

#phoneme_path: address of {.txt}
#ratio: split ratio
def train_valid_split(phoneme_path, ratio, seed):

    usage_list = open(os.path.join(phoneme_path, 'train_split.txt')).readlines()
    usage_list = [line.strip('\n') for line in usage_list]
    # generate random indices
    permuted_indices = torch.randperm(len(usage_list), generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)).tolist()
    usage_list = [usage_list[i] for i in permuted_indices]
    train_size = int(ratio * len(usage_list))
    train_list = usage_list[:train_size]
    valid_list = usage_list[train_size:]

    return train_list, valid_list


Since a phoneme may span several frames and is dependent to past and future frames, we should concatenate neighboring phonemes for training to achieve higher accuracy.


Code
# For the input tensor x shift n
def shift(x, n):
    if n < 0: # right shift
        left = x[0].repeat(-n, 1)
        right = x[:n]
    elif n > 0: # left shift
        right = x[-1].repeat(n, 1)
        left = x[n:]
    else:
        return x
    return torch.cat((left, right), dim=0)

# feature enhancement
def concat_feat(x, concat_n):
    assert concat_n % 2 == 1 # n must be odd
    if concat_n < 2:
        return x
    seq_len, feature_dim = len(x), len(x[0])
    x = x.repeat(1, concat_n) 
    x = x.view(seq_len, concat_n, feature_dim).permute(1, 0, 2)
    mid = (concat_n // 2)
    for r_idx in range(1, mid+1):
        x[mid + r_idx, :] = shift(x[mid + r_idx], r_idx)
        x[mid - r_idx, :] = shift(x[mid - r_idx], -r_idx)

    return x.permute(1, 0, 2).view(seq_len, concat_n * feature_dim)

    print(f"Shape of {split} feature is [nums, feature_nums]: {X.shape}")

class ImgDataset(Dataset):

class BasicBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, output_dim):
        super(BasicBlock, self).__init__()
        self.block = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, output_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.block(x)
        return x


class Classifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_layers, hidden_dim, output_dim=41):
        super(Classifier, self).__init__()
        
        self.layers = nn.Sequential(
            BasicBlock(input_dim, hidden_dim), # input_dim: 39 * concat_nframes
            *[BasicBlock(hidden_dim, hidden_dim) for _ in range(hidden_layers)],
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, output_dim) # 41 kinds of phoneme
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.layers(x)
        return out




Training Loop


Code
def trainer(train_loader, valid_loader, model, config, device):

    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()  # loss: CrossEntropyLoss
    #optimization algorithm (Adam). 
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=config['learning_rate']) 
    
    writer = SummaryWriter() # Writer of tensorboard.

    n_epochs, best_acc, step, early_stop_count = config['n_epochs'],0.0 , 0, 0

    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        model.train()
        epoch_start_time = time.time()
        loss_record = []
        train_acc = 0.0
        #x: features, y: labels
        for x, y in train_loader:
            optimizer.zero_grad()               # Set gradient to zero.
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)   # Move our data to device. 
            train_pred = model(x)  
            batch_loss = criterion(train_pred, y)
            batch_loss.backward()               # Compute gradient(back propagation).
            optimizer.step()                    # Update parameters.
            step += 1
            train_acc += np.sum(np.argmax(train_pred.detach().cpu().numpy(), axis=1) == y.cpu().numpy())
            loss_record.append(batch_loss.detach().item()) #detach(): separation gradient

        mean_train_loss = sum(loss_record)/len(loss_record)
        train_acc = train_acc / train_dataset.__len__()
        writer.add_scalar('Loss/train', mean_train_loss, step)
        writer.add_scalar('Accuracy/train', train_acc, step)

        model.eval() # Set our model to evaluation mode.
        loss_record = []
        valid_acc = 0.0
        with torch.no_grad():
            for x, y in valid_loader:
                x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
                valid_pred = model(x)
                batch_loss = criterion(valid_pred, y)
                valid_acc += np.sum(np.argmax(valid_pred.detach().cpu().numpy()
, axis=1) == y.cpu().numpy())
                loss_record.append(batch_loss.item())
            
            mean_valid_loss = sum(loss_record)/len(loss_record)
            valid_acc = valid_acc / valid_dataset.__len__()
            print('[%03d/%03d] %2.2f sec(s) Train Acc: %3.6f Loss: %3.6f | Val Acc: %3.6f loss: %3.6f' % \
              (epoch + 1, n_epochs, time.time() - epoch_start_time, \
               train_acc, mean_train_loss, valid_acc,
               mean_valid_loss))
            writer.add_scalar('Loss/valid', mean_valid_loss, step)
            writer.add_scalar('Accuracy/valid', valid_acc, step)

        if valid_acc > best_acc:
            best_acc = valid_acc
            torch.save(model.state_dict(), config['save_path']) # Save our best model
            print('Saving model with accuracy {:.3f}...'.format(best_acc))
            early_stop_count = 0
        else: 
            early_stop_count += 1

        if early_stop_count >= config['early_stop']:
            print('\nModel is not improving, so we halt the training session.')
            return

def download(name, cache_dir=os.path.join('..', 'data')):
    assert name in DATA_HUB, f"{name} is not existed in {DATA_HUB}"
    url, sha1_hash = DATA_HUB[name]
    os.makedirs(cache_dir, exist_ok=True)
    fname = os.path.join(cache_dir, url.split('/')[-1])
    if os.path.exists(fname):
        sha1 = hashlib.sha1()
        with open(fname, 'rb') as f:
            while True:
                data = f.read(1048576)
                if not data:
                    break
                sha1.update(data)
        if sha1.hexdigest() == sha1_hash:
            return fname  
    print(f'From {url} download {fname}...')
    r = requests.get(url, stream=True, verify=True)
    with open(fname, 'wb') as f:
        f.write(r.content)
    return fname

Dataset Processing
First, we apply a heuristic, replacing all missing values by the corresponding feature’s mean.
Next, we deal with discrete values. These include features such as “MSZoning”. We replace them by a one-hot encoding in the same way that we earlier transformed multi-class labels into vectors (see in Softmax Regression).
For instance, “MSZoning” assumes the values “RL” and “RM”. Dropping the “MSZoning” feature, two new indicator features “MSZoning_RL” and “MSZoning_RM” are created with values being either 0 or 1. According to one-hot encoding, if the original value of “MSZoning” is “RL”, then “MSZoning_RL” is 1 and “MSZoning_RM” is 0.

def preprocess(train_data, test_data):
    # Remove the ID and label columns
    label = 'SalePrice'
    all_features = pd.concat((train_data.iloc[:, 1:-1], test_data.iloc[:, 1:]))

    # Standardize numerical columns
    numeric_features = all_features.dtypes[all_features.dtypes != 'object'].index
    all_features[numeric_features] = all_features[numeric_features].apply(
    lambda x: (x - x.mean()) / (x.std()))
    # Replace NAN numerical features by 0
    all_features[numeric_features] = all_features[numeric_features].fillna(0)
    # Replace discrete features by one-hot encoding
    all_features = pd.get_dummies(all_features, dummy_na=True, dtype=int)
    print(f"Shape of all_features is {all_features.shape}")
    # Save preprocessed features
    n_train = train_data.shape[0]
    train_features = torch.tensor(all_features[:n_train].values, dtype=torch.float32)
    test_data = torch.tensor(all_features[n_train:].values, dtype=torch.float32)
    train_labels = torch.tensor(train_data.SalePrice.values.reshape(-1, 1), dtype=torch.float32)
    train_data = torch.cat([train_features, train_labels], dim=1)
    print("Shape of train_data is {}".format(train_data.shape))
    print("Shape of test_data is {}".format(test_data.shape))

#Split provided training data into training set and validation set
def train_valid_split(data_set, valid_ratio, seed):
    valid_set_size = int(valid_ratio * len(data_set)) 
    train_set_size = len(data_set) - valid_set_size
    train_set, valid_set = random_split(data_set, [train_set_size, valid_set_size], 
                                        generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed))

    train_set = np.array([data.numpy() for data in train_set])
    valid_set = np.array([data.numpy() for data in valid_set])

    return train_set, valid_set


train_data, valid_data = train_valid_split(train_data, config['valid_ratio'], config['seed'] )

In the next step, we should extract the features that are useful for our training from the dataset.
