#Selects useful features to perform regression
def select_feat(train_data, valid_data, test_data):
    label_train, label_valid = train_data[:,-1], valid_data[:,-1]
    feature_train, feature_valid, feature_test = train_data[:,:-1], valid_data[:,:-1], test_data
    feat_idx = list(range(len(feature_train[0])))
  
    return feature_train[:,feat_idx], feature_valid[:,feat_idx], feature_test[:,feat_idx], label_train, label_valid

# Select features
feature_train, feature_valid, feature_test, label_train, label_valid = select_feat(train_data, valid_data, test_data)

So, we’ve got three sets of data — train_data, valid_data, and test_data, and we’ve also got their features. Now, it’s time to construct our dataset.


Code
#x: Features.
#y: Targets, if none, do prediction.
class HousePriceDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, x, y=None):
        if y is None:
            self.y = y
        else:
            self.y = torch.FloatTensor(y)
        self.x = torch.FloatTensor(x)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        if self.y is None:
            return self.x[idx]
        else:
            return self.x[idx], self.y[idx]
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.x)

train_dataset, valid_dataset, test_dataset = HousePriceDataset(feature_train, label_train), \
                                            HousePriceDataset(feature_valid, label_valid), \
                                            HousePriceDataset(feature_test)

# Pytorch data loader loads pytorch dataset into batches.
train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=config['batch_size'], shuffle=True, pin_memory=True)
valid_loader = DataLoader(valid_dataset, batch_size=config['batch_size'], shuffle=True, pin_memory=True)
test_loader = DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size=config['batch_size'], shuffle=False, pin_memory=True)

for X,y in train_loader:
    print(f"Shape of X is {X.shape}\nShape of y is {y.shape}")
    break

At this point, we’ve finished building the dataset. With train_loader, we can get bulk data during the training process and pass it to the model. It’s time to construct our model.

title: Regression Task: House Prices Prediction
text:
Model
In Recognize Handwritten Digits by CNN, we adopt a network consisting of two convolutional layers and three fully connected layers. But in this task, we don’t need such a complex model that could cause overfitting.


Code
# Regression Model
class Regression(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim):
        super(Regression, self).__init__()
        self.layers = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, 128),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(128, 32),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(32, 1)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.layers(x)
        out = out.squeeze(1) # (B, 1) -> (B)
        return out


Our model consisting of three fully connected layers.
We use the logarithm of the price forecasts to measure the variance, rather than using the difference in forecasts directly, because we are concerned with relative quantities, not absolute quantities


Code
criterion = nn.MSELoss() # loss function. 

def log_rmse(pred, labels):
    clipped_preds = torch.clamp(pred, 1, float('inf'))
    rmse = torch.sqrt(criterion(torch.log(clipped_preds),
                           torch.log(labels)))
    return rmse.item()



Training Loop
We’ve got everything we need for training. Let’s get start our training process.


Code
def trainer(train_loader, valid_loader, model, config, device):
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=config['learning_rate'], weight_decay=0.1) 
    
    writer = SummaryWriter() # Writer of tensorboard.

    n_epochs, best_loss, step, early_stop_count = config['n_epochs'], math.inf, 0, 0

    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        model.train()
        loss_record = []

        for x, y in train_loader:
            optimizer.zero_grad()               # Set gradient to zero.
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)   # Move our data to device. 
            pred = model(x)            
            loss = criterion(pred, y)
            loss.backward()                     # Compute gradient(back propagation).
            optimizer.step()                    # Update parameters.
            step += 1
            loss_record.append(log_rmse(pred, y))

        mean_train_loss = sum(loss_record)/len(loss_record)
        writer.add_scalar('Loss/train', mean_train_loss, step)

        model.eval() # Set our model to evaluation mode.
        loss_record = []
        for x, y in valid_loader:
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
            with torch.no_grad():
                pred = model(x)
                loss = criterion(pred, y)

            loss_record.append(log_rmse(pred, y))
            
        mean_valid_loss = sum(loss_record)/len(loss_record)
        print(f'Epoch [{epoch+1}/{n_epochs}]: Train loss: {mean_train_loss:.4f}, Valid loss: {mean_valid_loss:.4f}')
        writer.add_scalar('Loss/valid', mean_valid_loss, step)

        if mean_valid_loss < best_loss:
            best_loss = mean_valid_loss
            torch.save(model.state_dict(), config['save_path']) # Save our best model
            print('Saving model with loss {:.3f}...'.format(best_loss))
            early_stop_count = 0
        else: 
            early_stop_count += 1

        if early_stop_count >= config['early_stop']:
            print('\nModel is not improving, so we halt the training session.')
            return




Start Training


Code
model = Regression(input_dim=feature_train.shape[1]).to(device) # put our model and data on the same computation device.
trainer(train_loader, valid_loader, model, config, device)

# Prediction
def predict(test_loader, model, device):

title: Introduction to Docker
text:
Using Images
When we run a container, if the images we need are not available locally, Docker will automatically download them from Docker image repositories.

List Images
We can use docker images in the terminal to list the images on the localhost.
PS C:\Users\hao> docker images

nvidia/cuda   12.6.3-cudnn-devel-ubuntu24.04   14802d3044a9   2 months ago   8.22GB

REPOSITORY: Source of images repository
TAG: Label of images
IMAGE ID: ID of images
CREATED: Created time
SIZE: Size of images



Get a New Image
When we use a non-existing image on the localhost, Docker will automatically download the image. If we want to download the image beforehand, we can use the docker pull command to download it. Once the download is complete, we can use the image to run the container directly.


Remove Images
If we want to remove a image, we can use docker rmi image_name.


Create a Image
If the image download from the docker images repositories cannot meet our needs, we can custom images by the followed methods:

Update the image from the already created container and commit the image

Step1: Using apt-get update in the running container to update the images. Step2: Using exit to exit the container.
Suppose that we have a container whose ID is e218edb10161, we can commit the copy of container by:
docker commit -m="has update" -a="runoob" e218edb10161 runoob/ubuntu:v2`
-m: Description of submission
-a: Images author
e218edb10161: ID of container
runoob/ubuntu:v2: Specify the name and label of the target image to be created
We can use docker images view our new image runoob/ubuntu:v2

Use the Dockerfile command to create a new image.

title: Introduction to Docker
text:
Using Container

Create Container
The following command activates a container using the ubuntu image with an argument to enter the container in command line mode:
docker run -it --gpus all --shm-size 128G -v /data1:/data1 -v /data2:/data2 -d --name arwin_cv IMAGE_name /bin/bash
-gpus all: Specifies to use all GPUs
The -shm-size: Allows us to specify the amount of shared memory available to the container. It provides higher access to allocated memory, thus allowing memory-intensive containers to run faster.
-v: mount directory, which is used to mount the host’s code directory and some configuration files inside the container.
-i: Interactive operation.
-t: Terminal.
IMAGE: Replace ubuntu image name.
/bin/bash: the command that comes after the image name, in this case we want to have an interactive shell, so we use /bin/bash.
We can use docker start <container-name-or-id> to activate the stopped container.
Here, we create our container by:
docker run --gpus all -it --name hao nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-cudnn-devel-ubuntu24.04 /bin/bash

title: Introduction to Docker
text:
Environment Migration
We have learned some basic operations about images and containerS. It’s time to create our deep learning container from the localhost conda environment.

Export Anaconda Environment
Step1: activate your Anaconda environment
conda activate <environment-name>
Step2: Export the environment
conda env export > environment.yml
We can obtain a .yml file that contains our anaconda environmental information.


Create Dockerfile
We introduced the method of creating a new image by Dockerfile, but we didn’t explain it in detail. Now, we use Dockerfile create our images.
First, we create a Dockerfile in the root directory.
Step1: FROM command can assign a base image that we pull from the official image repositories.
# base image
FROM nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-cudnn-devel-ubuntu24.04
Step2: Set Work Directory
WORKDIR /Hao
Step3: Install the Necessary Tools
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y wget git && apt-get clean

# Miniconda
ENV PATH="/opt/conda/bin:$PATH"
RUN wget https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh && \
    bash Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh -b -p /opt/conda && \
    rm -f Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh
Step4: Copy environment.yml to Container and Create Conda Env
COPY environment.yml /Hao/

RUN conda env create -f environment.yml && conda clean -afy
Step5: Activate Environment and Set Default Command
SHELL ["conda", "run", "-n", "<your-environment-name>", "/bin/bash", "-c"]

CMD ["bash"]


Create Images
We put the Dockerfile and environment.yml in the same directory and create the image.
docker build -t deep-learning-env:latest .

#check
docker images


Note
Many packages (e.g. winpty, vc, vs2015_runtime, ucrt, pywinpty) are specific to the Windows platform and therefore cannot be parsed in a Linux environment. When we migrate the anaconda environment from the Windows platform to docker it creates problems and we need to remove these packages from the environment.yml file.


Create Container
Running Container and Test:
docker run --gpus all -it --name hao_main my-deep-learning-env
